title: Accuracy vs. Interpretability in Designer-Level Fashion Classification
subtitle: Designer-level fashion classification with interpretability analysis
summary: Studied how model complexity and training strategies impact model performance on deisgner classification and model interpretability.

glance.oneLiner: A designer-level fashion classification study that contrasts accuracy with what models actually attend to and encode—under unmasked, masked, and augmentation-heavy training.
glance.problem: Designer labels on runway imagery can be predicted with high accuracy for the wrong reasons: models may exploit stable scene context (runway, lighting, venue cues) rather than garment attributes. The goal is to understand how model capacity affects both performance and the interpretability/semantic quality of learned representations when those shortcuts are reduced.
glance.approach: We compare ResNet-18/34/50 baselines (scratch and ImageNet-pretrained) against two lightweight FashionNet variants (Small ≈1M params, Medium ≈5M). We run three phases: (I) unmasked training to surface shortcut behavior, (II) DeepLabV3-ResNet-101 person segmentation to remove background context and force garment-centric learning, and (III) aggressive augmentation on unmasked data as a shortcut-suppression alternative. We analyze models with Grad-CAM and nearest-neighbor retrieval in embedding space.
glance.results: Unmasked training yields the best raw accuracy but often highlights runway/background regions in Grad-CAM. Masking shifts attention and nearest-neighbor structure toward garment attributes, but accuracy drops sharply for low-capacity models while larger/pretrained networks remain more robust. Augmentation partially reduces shortcut reliance and recovers some performance, but is less consistent than explicit background removal for producing garment-centric representations.
takeaways: High runway accuracy can reflect contextual shortcuts; interpretability is required to validate what is learned.
Segmentation-based masking is a strong shortcut breaker, but it exposes a capacity trade-off (small models degrade most).
Larger and/or pretrained models better preserve performance under reduced context and yield more semantically meaningful embeddings.
Augmentation can help, but it does not reliably substitute for explicit background removal.
Under reduced context, the feature space organizes around garment attributes (color/texture/silhouette), enabling analysis beyond label accuracy.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Fashion imagery combines strong visual structure—garments, textures, and silhouettes—with significant variation in pose, lighting, styling, and scene context. This tension between structure and abstraction makes fine-grained classification challenging, while raising a deeper question: what visual cues do models actually learn when performing fashion recognition?

This project investigates how model capacity influences both classification accuracy and interpretability in designer-level fashion classification. We ask three guiding questions: how complex a model must be to achieve strong performance, how much capacity is required to learn meaningful and interpretable representations, and how those representations can be used to analyze fashion itself.

We compare several ResNet baselines against a lightweight custom architecture and examine learned features using Grad-CAM and feature-space retrieval. Early experiments reveal that highly accurate models often rely on contextual shortcuts, particularly runway backgrounds and scene cues. To isolate garment-centric signals, we apply DeepLab-based segmentation to remove background context, reframing the task as a test of representation learning under reduced contextual bias.

By forcing models to encode images primarily through garment-level features rather than background correlations, this setup enables a more faithful examination of the learned feature space. The resulting embeddings exhibit emergent structure that reflects visual similarity in fashion, offering insight into what models consider “similar” beyond label accuracy alone. In hindsight, this analysis also highlights the limitations of designer classification as a pretext task, motivating future work toward more self-supervised and fashion-centric objectives.

callout.label: Key finding
callout.text: High accuracy on runway images often comes from background and scene shortcuts, not garment understanding. Background removal exposes a capacity-dependent trade-off: larger/pretrained models retain more performance while learning cleaner, garment-centric representations; augmentation helps, but segmentation is the more reliable shortcut breaker.

sections.title: Dataset
paragraphs: We use the iDesigner FGVC dataset from CVPR 2019: 50,000 high-resolution runway images labeled by designer across major fashion houses. The diversity of designers makes the task visually rich and fine-grained, while the standard crop keeps substantial runway context around the model.

We found models (CNN model) often relied on background cues such as runway textures, lighting, and venue architecture rather than garment details. This motivated a background-subtracted variant so performance would reflect garment-level understanding.
We applied a DeepLab person-segmentation model (trained on COCO) to produce binary masks, remove background pixels, and retain only the model and garments for analysis.
This segmented dataset provides a cleaner foundation for evaluating the link between model capacity, interpretability, and true visual understanding of fashion features.

sections.title: Model Architectures
paragraphs: We evaluate three families of CNNs: ResNet-18/34/50 baselines and two lightweight custom models, FashionNet-Small and FashionNet-Medium.

The FashionNet models are lightweight, purpose-built convolutional architectures designed to study the relationship between model capacity and representation quality. Both variants follow a simple stem-and-stages design, progressively increasing channel width while reducing spatial resolution to move from local texture cues to more global, silhouette-level structure. Global average pooling is used to produce compact feature embeddings, followed by a single linear classifier for designer prediction. The Medium variant widens and slightly deepens each stage relative to the Small model, increasing representational capacity while preserving the same overall architectural philosophy. sections.title: Methods Overview
paragraphs: Our methodology is organized as a sequence of increasingly constrained training regimes, each motivated by observations from the preceding stage. Across all experiments, we maintain a shared training and evaluation protocol to isolate the effects of architectural choice and data treatment.
Phase I: Unmasked Baselines

We begin by training all models on unmodified runway images to establish a performance baseline and assess shortcut behavior under standard conditions. This phase reveals that high-capacity models achieve strong accuracy but frequently rely on background and scene context, as evidenced by attention maps and feature similarity patterns.
This initial stage motivates the remainder of the study by exposing the tension between raw accuracy and meaningful representation learning.
Phase II: Masked, Garment-Centric Training

This phase reframes designer classification as a test of representation quality under reduced contextual bias. Masked training provides a cleaner lens for interpretability analysis, revealing how different architectures encode texture, shape, and silhouette when background shortcuts are no longer available.
Phase III: Augmentation-Driven Shortcut Suppression

As a complementary strategy, we explore whether aggressive data augmentation on unmasked images can mitigate background dependence without explicit segmentation. Models are trained with strong spatial and photometric perturbations, including random crops and rescaling, heavy color jitter, perspective transforms, multi-scale random erasing, and coarse noise masks.
This phase probes whether robustness-inducing augmentations can approximate the benefits of masking while preserving the full visual scene.
Training and Evaluation

All models are trained using cross-entropy loss with either SGD or Adam, over approximately 40 epochs, with step or cosine learning-rate schedules selected for stability. Performance is evaluated using top-1 validation accuracy, while interpretability is assessed through Grad-CAM visualizations and nearest-neighbor retrieval in feature space. Additional occlusion analyses yielded consistent qualitative trends and are omitted for brevity.

sections.title: Results: Phase I (Unmasked)
paragraphs: On the unmasked dataset, pretrained ResNet-50 achieves the best accuracy, and pretraining consistently boosts all ResNet baselines. When trained from scratch, both FashionNet variants outperform scratch ResNets, suggesting the lightweight models readily exploit stable dataset cues.

afterTableParagraphs: Grad-CAM reveals those gains are not garment-centric: activations frequently concentrate on runway floor, lighting gradients, and peripheral context rather than the clothing. This indicates strong background–label correlations and motivates masking in Phase II.

sections.title: Results: Phase II (Masked)
paragraphs: Masking removes runway context and forces reliance on garment shape, texture, and silhouette. Accuracy drops sharply across all models; pretrained ResNets remain most robust, while FashionNet-Small and Medium degrade toward chance, signaling capacity limits under garment-only cues.

tables.title: Table III: Validation accuracy (%) on the masked dataset

afterTableParagraphs: Grad-CAM shifts toward the garment even when masked-trained models are evaluated on unmasked images, suggesting masking encourages less context-dependent representations.

figures.caption: Figure IV: Grad-CAM result on masked images.

sections.title: Results: Phase III (Heavy Augmentation)
paragraphs: Heavy augmentation on unmasked images recovers much of the performance lost in the masked setting. Pretrained ResNets remain strong; FashionNet-Medium improves more reliably than FashionNet-Small, indicating modest capacity helps benefit from augmentation.

tables.title: Table IV: Validation accuracy (%) with strong augmentation on unmasked data

afterTableParagraphs: Grad-CAM shows only partial mitigation: attention moves somewhat toward garments, but runway and scene regions still contribute, implying residual contextual shortcuts.

figures.caption: Figure V: Grad-CAM comparisons with heavy augmentation.

sections.title: Feature-Space Interpretability
paragraphs: To probe what the model learns beyond accuracy, we run nearest-neighbor retrieval in feature space using FashionNet-Medium trained on the masked dataset. We extract penultimate-layer embeddings, normalize them, and compare examples with cosine similarity to retrieve top neighbors from the training set, showing both ground-truth and predicted designer labels.

Across examples, neighbors often share color palettes, fabric textures, silhouettes, and overall aesthetic structure with the query, even when designer labels differ. Similar layering, drape, or pattern geometry appears repeatedly, suggesting the representation organizes images by visually salient garment attributes rather than coarse scene context. The Figure(s) below shows representative matches.

Importantly, these embeddings come from a model trained only on masked images but evaluated on the original unmasked dataset. Even with background restored, neighbor structure remains garment-focused, reinforcing that masking trades off accuracy but yields a more semantically meaningful feature space for fashion analysis.

figures.caption: Figure VI–IX: Feature-space retrieval examples (color similarity; pattern/texture similarity).

afterParagraphs: Taken together, this analysis reframes designer classification not as an end goal, but as a vehicle for studying how visual representations emerge under different training constraints. By stripping away contextual shortcuts, the model is encouraged to organize images around garment-level attributes such as color, texture, structure, and silhouette, i.e. properties that align more closely with how fashion is perceived and compared. While this comes at a cost to raw classification accuracy, the resulting feature space offers a clearer window into what the model has learned, revealing structure that is visually meaningful rather than label-driven. In this sense, the project serves less as a benchmark on designer recognition and more as a controlled experiment in representation learning for fashion imagery.

sections.title: Takeaways
bullets: Designer classification can look solved on runway data while models still lean on scene context; interpretability checks are necessary.
Segmentation-based masking is a strong intervention for reducing contextual bias, but it makes capacity limits visible—small models lose accuracy sharply.
Larger and/or pretrained models are more resilient under garment-only cues and produce more semantically meaningful embeddings for retrieval.
Heavy augmentation reduces shortcut reliance somewhat, but it does not consistently substitute for explicit background removal.

The most interesting output is the learned feature space: under reduced context, it organizes images by garment attributes (texture, color, silhouette), suggesting more fashion-centric objectives beyond designer labels.
